As a wizard and scholar of Middle-earth, I have been studying the magic of the natural world for centuries. Through my self-portraits, I aim to capture the essence of my own being and reflect on my own journey through time. Each photograph is a reflection of my own experiences and emotions. Through my photography, I hope to offer a glimpse into my life as a scholar and adventurer, and inspire others to reflect on their own journeys through the world.

title: BMI and Systolic Blood Pressure in U.S. Adults
text:
This analysis examines the relationship between body mass index (BMI) and systolic blood pressure among adults ages 21–79 in the 2017–March 2020 NHANES sample. BMI was selected as the primary exposure, and mean systolic blood pressure was selected as the outcome. Age and sex were also examined as additional variables that may be associated with systolic blood pressure.
I hypothesized that higher BMI would be associated with higher systolic blood pressure.


The full results and visualizations from this analysis are available in the interactive dashboard.

title: BMI and Systolic Blood Pressure in U.S. Adults
text:
Data Preparation
Data were obtained from the 2017–March 2020 NHANES pre-pandemic files. I used the demographic, body measures, and blood pressure examination files. The files were joined using the participant identifier (SEQN).
The analytic sample was restricted to examined participants ages 21–79. BMI was obtained from the body measures data, while systolic blood pressure was calculated as the mean of up to three available systolic blood pressure measurements. Missing values were retained rather than removing participants from the full dataset.

title: BMI and Systolic Blood Pressure in U.S. Adults
text:
Descriptive Analysis
The final analytic dataset contained 7,853 participants. The mean age was 49.3 years, the mean BMI was 30.2 kg/m², and the mean systolic blood pressure was 124.1 mmHg.
I first examined the relationship between BMI and systolic blood pressure using a scatterplot with a fitted linear regression line. Because both variables are quantitative, the scatterplot allows the individual observations and overall direction of the relationship to be examined without categorizing either variable.
I also examined age in relation to systolic blood pressure using a scatterplot and compared the distribution of systolic blood pressure between males and females using a boxplot.

title: BMI and Systolic Blood Pressure in U.S. Adults
text:
Regression Analysis
I first fit a simple linear regression model with systolic blood pressure as the outcome and BMI as the predictor. I then fit an adjusted linear regression model including BMI, age, and sex. The adjusted model was used to examine the association between BMI and systolic blood pressure while accounting for age and sex.

title: BMI and Systolic Blood Pressure in U.S. Adults
text:
Results
In the unadjusted model, a one-unit increase in BMI was associated with approximately 0.09 mmHg higher systolic blood pressure. Although this association was statistically significant (p = 0.0024), BMI alone explained very little of the variation in systolic blood pressure (R² = 0.001).
After adjusting for age and sex, the association between BMI and systolic blood pressure remained positive. A one-unit increase in BMI was associated with approximately 0.10 mmHg higher systolic blood pressure (p = 0.0003), holding age and sex constant.
Age showed a stronger positive association with systolic blood pressure. Each additional year of age was associated with approximately 0.48 mmHg higher systolic blood pressure (p < 0.0001). Females had approximately 5.03 mmHg lower systolic blood pressure than males (p < 0.0001), holding BMI and age constant. The adjusted model explained approximately 19.2% of the variation in systolic blood pressure.

title: BMI and Systolic Blood Pressure in U.S. Adults
text:
Conclusion
The results supported my hypothesis that higher BMI would be associated with higher systolic blood pressure, although the magnitude of this association was small. The relationship between age and systolic blood pressure was substantially stronger in this sample, and systolic blood pressure also differed by sex.
These findings show why it is useful to consider additional characteristics when examining the relationship between BMI and blood pressure. Because this analysis used observational NHANES data, the results describe associations and should not be interpreted as evidence that BMI causes changes in systolic blood pressure.

Welcome to my website!
I am Chloe Relf, an MPH student at Case Western Reserve University, where I am studying population health research. I also received my bachelor’s degree from Case, majoring in Economics and Psychology with additional coursework in biology and chemistry.
I currently work in the Samuels Laboratory at the Louis Stokes Cleveland VA Medical Center, where I contribute to research on diabetic retinopathy using mouse models. My research experience has included laboratory techniques such as PCR, immunohistochemistry, and electroretinography, as well as work examining the biological mechanisms underlying retinal disease.
My current interests involve expanding from laboratory-based health research toward population-level questions in epidemiology and health economics. I am particularly interested in zoonotic and vector-borne diseases, disease risk and prevention, and the ways economic and healthcare systems influence population health outcomes. Through my MPH training, I am developing quantitative and epidemiologic skills that I hope to apply to these areas in future research.
Please feel free to contact me if you have any questions or would like to discuss potential projects.
